subject: chemistry
title: Polymers and plastics
summary: How monomers join to make polymers by addition polymerisation, everyday plastics, the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets, and recycling and environmental issues.
body:
Look around and you will find plastics everywhere: drink bottles, phone cases, pipes, clothing fibres and food wrap. All of these are **polymers**, giant molecules built from many small repeating units. Understanding how polymers form and why they behave so differently helps explain why some plastics can be melted and recycled while others cannot, and why plastic waste is such a big environmental issue.

## Think of it like this

### Addition polymerisation is like a conga line at a party

Imagine each person at a party has both hands holding their own drink – that's a **monomer** like ethene, with its C=C **double bond**. To join the conga line, each person lets go with one hand (one bond of the double bond breaks) and uses it to grab the next person. Thousands of people joining up make one huge line – the **polymer**. Nobody leaves the party in the process, just as no atoms are lost in **addition polymerisation**, and the pattern that keeps repeating along the line is the **repeating unit**.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* people in a conga line can let go and walk off, but the new C–C single bonds in a polymer are strong covalent bonds that don't easily come apart.

### LDPE and HDPE are like a pile of branches versus a packet of dry spaghetti

Twiggy branches with lots of side bits can't pack neatly, so a pile of them is loose and springy. That's **low-density polyethene (LDPE)**: its chains have many side branches, so they can't pack closely, making it soft and flexible like cling wrap. Straight sticks of dry spaghetti pack tightly into a solid bundle. That's **high-density polyethene (HDPE)**: few branches, tightly packed chains, so it's stronger and more rigid, like a milk bottle.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* real polymer chains are not stiff sticks – they're long, flexible and tangled, and they can coil and fold.

### Thermoplastics versus thermosets: cooked noodles versus a knotted fishing net

A bowl of cooked noodles is a tangle of long strands that can slide past each other when you stir it. **Thermoplastics** are like that: the chains are held together only by weak forces, so heating lets them slide, the plastic softens and melts, and it can be remoulded and **recycled**. A fishing net has strands knotted to each other all over. **Thermosets** have strong covalent **cross-links** joining chains into a rigid network, so heating can't make the chains slide apart – the plastic doesn't melt, and eventually it chars.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* noodles slide at any temperature, but a thermoplastic is solid at room temperature and only flows once it has been heated enough to overcome the forces between the chains.

### In real life

The number inside the triangle on the bottom of a plastic bottle is the **resin identification code**, which helps sort thermoplastics for recycling. Saucepan handles and power-point sockets are made from thermosets because they need to stay hard when hot, and microplastics found at beaches come from bigger plastic items breaking into tiny pieces.

## Key ideas

### Monomers and polymers

A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join to many other identical (or similar) molecules. A **polymer** is a very long molecule made by joining thousands of monomers together in a chain. The process of joining monomers is called **polymerisation**.

A useful picture is a string of paperclips: each paperclip is a monomer, and the long chain is the polymer.

Polymers can be **natural**, such as starch, cellulose, proteins, rubber and wool, or **synthetic** (made by people), such as polyethene and nylon. Synthetic polymers are often made from chemicals obtained from crude oil.

### Addition polymerisation

In **addition polymerisation**, monomers that contain a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) join together. Alkenes such as ethene are the classic example.

How it happens:

1. One of the two bonds in each C=C double bond breaks.
2. The freed bonding electrons are used to make new single bonds to the neighbouring monomers.
3. This repeats thousands of times, forming a long chain held together by single C–C bonds.

Nothing is lost in the reaction: every atom in the monomers ends up in the polymer. That is why it is called "addition".

For ethene forming polyethene:

`n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–`

Here n is a very large number, often thousands. The part in brackets is the **repeating unit**: the section of the chain that repeats over and over. Notice the polymer has no double bond, because the double bonds were used to link the monomers.

### Naming addition polymers

The name is simply "poly" plus the name of the monomer, often in brackets:

| Monomer | Polymer | Common name | Everyday uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| ethene, CH₂=CH₂ | poly(ethene) | polyethylene, PE | shopping bags, bottles, cling wrap |
| propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃ | poly(propene) | polypropylene, PP | containers, ropes, bottle caps |
| chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl | poly(chloroethene) | PVC | water pipes, cable insulation |
| phenylethene (styrene) | poly(phenylethene) | polystyrene | foam packaging, cups |
| tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂ | poly(tetrafluoroethene) | PTFE | non-stick pan coatings |

To draw the repeating unit from a monomer, change the C=C to C–C, keep the other atoms in the same positions, and add bonds sticking out of each side through the brackets.

### Low-density and high-density polyethene

The same monomer can give polymers with different properties depending on how the chains are arranged. **Low-density polyethene (LDPE)** has many side branches, so its chains cannot pack closely. This makes it soft and flexible, good for plastic bags and cling wrap. **High-density polyethene (HDPE)** has few branches, so its chains pack tightly. It is stronger and more rigid, good for milk bottles and buckets. The conditions used in the factory decide which type forms.

### Thermoplastics and thermosets

The way chains are held together decides what happens when a plastic is heated.

**Thermoplastics** are made of long chains that are held to each other only by weak forces between the chains. There are no strong bonds linking one chain to another. When heated, the chains can slide past each other, so the plastic softens and melts. On cooling, it hardens again. This can be repeated, so thermoplastics can be remoulded and recycled. Polyethene, polypropylene and PVC are thermoplastics.

**Thermosets** (thermosetting polymers) have strong covalent bonds, called **cross-links**, joining neighbouring chains into a rigid network. When heated, the chains cannot slide apart. Instead of melting, a thermoset stays hard until it eventually chars or burns. Once set, it cannot be remoulded. Thermosets are used for electrical sockets, saucepan handles, kitchen benchtops and some glues (such as epoxy resins), where heat resistance matters.

| Property | Thermoplastic | Thermoset |
|---|---|---|
| Bonds between chains | weak forces only | strong covalent cross-links |
| Effect of heating | softens and melts | does not melt; chars |
| Can be remoulded? | yes | no |
| Easy to recycle? | yes, by melting | no |

### Recycling and environmental issues

Most synthetic polymers are not **biodegradable**: microorganisms cannot easily break them down, so they can last for hundreds of years in landfill or the ocean. Plastic waste harms wildlife that swallow it or become tangled in it. Over time, large pieces break into tiny fragments called **microplastics**, which spread through water, soil and food chains.

Ways to reduce the problem include:

- **Reduce and reuse**: using fewer single-use plastics, such as by carrying reusable bags and bottles.
- **Mechanical recycling**: sorting thermoplastics by type, washing, melting and remoulding them into new products. Plastics carry a **resin identification code** (a number inside a triangle) to help sorting. Each time a plastic is recycled, its chains can get shorter, so quality often drops.
- **Burning for energy**: releases energy but also produces carbon dioxide and possibly toxic gases.
- **Bioplastics**: polymers made from plant materials, some of which are biodegradable under the right conditions.

Because most plastics are made from crude oil, a non-renewable resource, recycling also helps conserve it.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Drawing the polymer of propene

Show the formation of the polymer from propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃.

- Step 1: Break one bond of the C=C. The two carbons now each have a free bond.
- Step 2: The CH₃ group stays attached to its carbon as a side branch.
- Step 3: Write the repeating unit in brackets with bonds sticking out.

`n CH₂=CH(CH₃) → –(CH₂–CH(CH₃))ₙ–`

The polymer is poly(propene), with a CH₃ branch on every second carbon of the chain.

### Example 2: Identifying the monomer

A polymer has the repeating unit –(CH₂–CHCl)–. Name the monomer.

- Step 1: Put the double bond back between the two carbons of the repeating unit: CH₂=CHCl.
- Step 2: This is ethene with one hydrogen replaced by chlorine: chloroethene.
- The polymer is poly(chloroethene), PVC.

## Common mistakes

- Drawing the polymer with a C=C double bond still in it. The double bond is used up in linking.
- Thinking addition polymerisation produces a by-product such as water. All atoms end up in the polymer.
- Saying thermosets melt at high temperatures. They do not melt; they char.
- Confusing the monomer (a small molecule) with the repeating unit (part of the chain, with single bonds only).
- Saying "plastics" are all recyclable. Thermosets cannot be melted and remoulded.

## Exam tips

- When explaining thermoplastic and thermoset properties, always mention whether there are cross-links between chains.
- Draw repeating units with brackets and with bonds passing through the brackets on both sides.
- In environmental questions, give specific issues (non-biodegradable, microplastics, made from non-renewable crude oil) and specific solutions.

## Tips to remember

- **Picture a chain of paperclips.** Each paperclip is a monomer, and the long chain is the polymer.
- **Addition means nothing is lost.** Every atom in the monomers ends up in the polymer, with no water or other by-product.
- **The double bond "opens its arms".** One bond of the C=C breaks so each carbon can hold hands with its neighbours. So the repeating unit has only single bonds, with bonds sticking out through the brackets.
- **Naming is easy: "poly" + monomer name.** Ethene → poly(ethene), chloroethene → poly(chloroethene) (PVC).
- **Thermoplastic = chocolate; thermoset = baked cake.** Chocolate melts and can be reshaped again and again. Heat won't turn a cake back into batter, because cross-links lock the chains, so it chars instead of melting.
- **LDPE vs HDPE:** branched chains pack loosely like a messy pile of sticks (soft bags). Straight chains pack tightly like stacked logs (strong milk bottles).

## Key terms

- **Monomer** — a small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer.
- **Polymer** — a very long molecule made of many repeating monomer units.
- **Polymerisation** — the process of joining monomers to form a polymer.
- **Addition polymerisation** — polymerisation of monomers with a C=C double bond, with no other product formed.
- **Repeating unit** — the part of a polymer chain that repeats.
- **Thermoplastic** — a polymer with no cross-links that softens and melts when heated.
- **Thermoset** — a polymer with covalent cross-links that does not melt when heated.
- **Cross-link** — a covalent bond joining two polymer chains.
- **Biodegradable** — able to be broken down by microorganisms.
- **Microplastics** — tiny plastic fragments that spread through the environment.

## Summary

- Polymers are long chains of many monomers joined together.
- Addition polymerisation joins monomers that have a C=C double bond, forming single bonds and no by-product.
- The polymer's name is "poly" plus the monomer's name.
- Thermoplastics have no cross-links and can be melted and recycled; thermosets have cross-links and do not melt.
- Most plastics are non-biodegradable, so reducing, reusing and recycling are important.

questions.prompt: What feature must a monomer have to take part in addition polymerisation?
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation works by breaking one bond of a C=C double bond so monomers can link. A chlorine atom is tempting because PVC's monomer has one, but ethene has no chlorine and still polymerises.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the polymer formed from propene?
questions.explanation: The polymer name is 'poly' plus the monomer name, so propene forms poly(propene), also called polypropylene. Polyethene is made from ethene. Propane is the alkane with three carbons and is not a polymer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about addition polymerisation is correct?

options.A: Water is released each time two monomers join
options.B: The polymer chain still contains C=C double bonds
options.C: The polymer has a much higher mass than the monomers that formed it
options.D: All the atoms of the monomers end up in the polymer

questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation nothing else is produced, so every atom ends up in the polymer. Option C is tempting, but the total mass of polymer equals the total mass of the monomers that joined (mass is conserved). The double bonds become single bonds in the chain.

questions.prompt: Why do thermoplastics soften when heated, while thermosets do not?

options.A: Thermoplastics have no strong cross-links between chains, so chains can slide past each other
options.B: Thermoplastics have shorter chains than thermosets
options.C: Thermosets contain double bonds that resist heat

questions.explanation: In a thermoplastic the chains are held together only by weak forces, so heating lets them slide apart. Thermosets have covalent cross-links that lock the chains in place. Option B is tempting but chain length is not the key difference.

questions.prompt: A polymer has the repeating unit –(CF₂–CF₂)–. What is its monomer?
questions.explanation: Putting the double bond back between the two carbons gives CF₂=CF₂, tetrafluoroethene, the monomer of PTFE. CF₃–CF₃ is tempting but has no double bond, so it cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

questions.prompt: Why is low-density polyethene (LDPE) softer and more flexible than high-density polyethene (HDPE)?

options.A: LDPE is made from a different monomer
options.B: LDPE has cross-links between its chains
options.C: LDPE chains have many branches, so they cannot pack closely together

questions.explanation: Both are made from ethene. LDPE's branched chains pack loosely, making it softer. Cross-links (option B) would make a polymer more rigid, not more flexible.

questions.prompt: Which material would be best for the handle of a frying pan?

options.A: Polyethene, because it is a thermoplastic
options.B: A thermoset, because it does not melt when heated
options.C: A thermoplastic, because it can be remoulded
options.D: Polystyrene foam, because it is light

questions.explanation: A pan handle gets hot, so it needs a material that keeps its shape when heated. A thermoset's cross-links stop it softening. Option C is tempting because recyclability sounds good, but a thermoplastic handle would soften when hot.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an environmental problem caused by plastics?

options.A: Plastics dissolve in sea water and change its pH
options.B: Plastics break down quickly in landfill, releasing oxygen
options.C: Thermosets are easier to recycle than thermoplastics
options.D: Most plastics are not biodegradable and break into microplastics that spread through ecosystems

questions.explanation: Most synthetic polymers resist breakdown by microorganisms and fragment into microplastics. Option C is the reverse of the truth: thermoplastics can be melted and recycled, but thermosets cannot.
